Away
uh-WAY
adv.
Webster 1828 points AWAY to way: absent; at a distance; much used with verbs of going or sending from; as an exclamation, a command to depart (Away with him); and in the older phrase I cannot away with it, I cannot bear it. This page fills the KJV-gap adverb. Companion pages already treat depart, pass, and word. The noun way is a separate head.

Biblical Definition

Away in Scripture is not a mood of distance. It is removal, departure, or the thing that will not be removed. John the Baptist does not offer a milder Lamb: Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world (John 1:29). Jesus will not let creation outlast His speech: Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away (Matt 24:35). He will not let the Eleven treat His going as abandonment: It is expedient for you that I go away: for if I go not away, the Comforter will not come unto you (John 16:7). The last city is not therapy; it is subtraction of death: God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes — for the former things are passed away (Rev 21:4). He will not let marriage be dissolved at will: Whosoever shall put away his wife, except it be for fornication, and shall marry another, committeth adultery (Matt 19:9). The dictionary therefore keeps away from becoming a slogan of self-care exits. It is the Bible’s way of saying: this is taken off, this departs, this must not be sent off.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines AWAY as absent, at a distance; used with verbs of going or sending from; as an exclamation, a command to depart (Away with him); and in I cannot away with it, I cannot bear or endure it (Isaiah 1).

expand to see more

AWA'Y, adverb [See Way.]

1. Absent; at a distance; as, the master is away from home. Have me away for I am wounded. 2 Chronicles 35:23.

2. It is much used with words signifying moving or going from; as, go away, send away, run away, etc.; all signifying departure, or separation to a distance. Sometimes without the verb; as, whither away so fast.

3. As an exclamation, it is a command or invitation to depart; away, that is, be gone, or let us go. Away with him. Take him away.

5. Away with has a peculiar signification in the phrase, I cannot away with it. The sense is, I cannot bear or endure it.

Key Scripture

John 1:29 — "The next day John seeth Jesus coming unto him, and saith, Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world."

Matthew 24:35 — "Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away."

John 16:7 — "Nevertheless I tell you the truth; It is expedient for you that I go away: for if I go not away, the Comforter will not come unto you; but if I depart, I will send him unto you."

Revelation 21:4 — "And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain: for the former things are passed away."

Matthew 19:9 — "And I say unto you, Whosoever shall put away his wife, except it be for fornication, and shall marry another, committeth adultery: and whoso marrieth her which is put away doth commit adultery."

Modern Corruption

Away is corrupted when taking away sin is recast as taking away shame, when heaven and earth passing away is used to relativize Christ’s words, and when putting away a wife is treated as a private exit rather than adultery except for fornication.

expand to see more

The first corruption is to hear John 1:29 as relief from embarrassment. The Lamb taketh away the sin of the world — guilt before God, not a bruise to self-regard. Therapeutic religion prefers a lamb who takes away low self-image. John points at Jesus as sin-bearer.

The second corruption is to invert Matthew 24:35. Modern talk lets Scripture pass away with cultures while the earth is treated as the lasting thing. Jesus says the opposite. Heaven and earth go. His words do not.

The third corruption is to make Matthew 19:9 a lifestyle clause. No-fault exits keep the verb and lose the exception. He names putting away and remarriage as adultery, save for fornication. The recovery is the creational bond, not a softer adverb of departure.

A fourth corruption is to treat John 16:7 as divine absence. The Son goes away in order that the Comforter come. Cessationist recovery still confesses the Spirit sent; it does not turn the going into a hole where private revelation must rush in.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Webster: see Way. Verse-cache Strong’s on the quotations below: Greek airo (G142) at John 1:29 (taketh away); Greek parerchomai (G3928) at Matthew 24:35; Greek aperchomai (G565) at John 16:7; Greek exaleipho (G1813) at Revelation 21:4 (wipe away); Greek apoluo (G630) at Matthew 19:9 (put away). Isaiah 53:6 leaves English away untagged in this cache (the verse uses astray / turned); no Hebrew number is minted from that line for this adverb.

expand to see more

Greek airo (G142) — to lift, take up, take away (John 1:29, taketh away the sin).

Greek parerchomai (G3928) — to pass by, pass away (Matt 24:35).

Greek aperchomai (G565) — to go away, depart (John 16:7).

Greek exaleipho (G1813) — to wipe off, wipe away (Rev 21:4); Greek apoluo (G630) — to loose, send away, put away (Matt 19:9).

Isaiah 53:6 untagged on English away in this cache — no Hebrew number is invented for this page from that verse.

Usage

"The Lamb taketh away the sin of the world (John 1:29) — sin, not embarrassment."

"Heaven and earth shall pass away; His words shall not (Matt 24:35)."

"He goes away that the Comforter may come (John 16:7); putting away a wife except for fornication is adultery (Matt 19:9)."
